newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL overnight at 8.4/5 pct after payment for bills.
newsitem.headline: KL overnight at 8.4/5 pct after payment for bills.

text.p: The overnight interbank rate was steady at 8.4/5 percent around 0800 GMT as the market tightened after banks paid out one billion ringgit for two Bank Negara bill issues, dealers said on Wednesday.
They said there was an outgo of 500 million ringgit from the banking system due to the issues. The issues were partly paid for by a maturing 500 million ringgit Bank Negara bill issue.
Dealers said the overnight opened at around 7.5 percent and was expected to end above 8.0 percent.
Earlier, most interbank rates were firm across the board due to the payment for Bank Negara bills.
The outflow coupled with a steady draining of foreign funds from Malaysia had tightened the market and pushed up rates.
One foreign bank dealer said some foreign banks, which are normally lenders, were also running short.
One-week money was at 7.80/90 percent against 7.70/80, two-week was at 7.70/80 percent against 7.40/50 and three-week was unchanged at 7.35/40 percent.
One-month to one-year were all trading between 7.35 and 7.45 percent, the dealers said.
Dealers said there was market talk that foreign funds were withdrawing from Malaysia, both from deposits and from the stock market, which has been falling sharply recently.
"Some say the funds are moving from Malaysia to Latin America," said the head of money dealing at a Malaysian bank.
He said the rising interest rates was in line with Bank Negara's tight monetary policy stance, though the ringgit's decline was some cause for worry.
Dealers said there was unlikely to be any change in the domestic market situation over the next few days.
"There are no expected inflows, unless the direction of the ringgit changes," a dealer with another Malaysian bank said.
Last week, Bank Negara intervened to slow the ringgit's fall by selling nearly $200 million, dealers said. A 500-million ringgit Bank Negara bill issue also reduced liquidity in the flush market.
"With ringgit still under pressure to weaken, and stock market in the doldrums, there is bound to be more funds going out of Malaysia," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.
But, interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange were steady across the board just ahead of the lunch break.
At 0800 GMT, three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate-based (KLIBOR) June contract was at 92.68, or an implied yield of 7.32 percent.
September was at 92.67, or 7.33 percent and December at 92.60, or 7.40 percent.
March 1998 contract was unchanged at 92.48 and June at 92.47.
-- Madhav Reddy (603-230 7509) .
